interviewQuestions.question: Design an image hosting service like Imgur.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point out upfront that the upload form is the easy part — the real design is dedup and derivative serving at billions-of-images scale. Uploads get hashed on their actual bytes (content-addressable storage), so identical images from different users store once; a small reference layer tracks who's using each object so one user's delete doesn't remove bytes another still needs.

For serving, I'd precompute the handful of sizes almost every image needs (thumbnail, feed) at upload time, and generate anything less common on the fly, caching the result so the second request for that size is fast. All of it sits behind a CDN whose cache key includes size and format, not just image ID, so a thumbnail request can never return a full-size image.

I'd close on read:write ratio — images are written once and read constantly, so nearly all the optimization budget belongs on the read path.

**Testing:** whether you identify dedup and derivative strategy as the actual hard problems instead of over-engineering the upload flow.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: End-to-end design like Imgur

interviewQuestions.question: How would you avoid storing the same image twice when millions of users upload overlapping content, like memes or stock photos?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use content-addressable storage: hash each upload's actual bytes (SHA-256 is fine) and use that hash as the storage key. Two uploads with identical bytes hash identically, so the second upload just adds a reference to the existing object instead of writing new bytes — this catches true duplicates regardless of filename or upload source.

The subtlety is lifecycle: I'd keep a reference count or per-user ownership record alongside the shared object, so deleting one user's copy only removes their reference, not the underlying bytes other users still point at. I'd also do the dedup check before any storage write, since checking after already writing defeats the savings.

**Testing:** whether you know the mechanism (content hashing) and its main gotcha (shared ownership on delete), not just the phrase 'deduplication'.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Deduplication strategy at scale

interviewQuestions.question: Should you precompute every image size you might ever need, or generate them on demand?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as storage cost versus latency, and reject both extremes. Precomputing everything wastes storage on sizes rarely or never requested, since the multiplier compounds across billions of images. Generating everything on demand pushes latency onto every single request, including the handful of sizes that account for most traffic.

My actual answer is a hybrid: precompute the few sizes nearly every image gets requested at (thumbnail, feed, detail), and handle anything else on the fly, caching the generated derivative so only the first request for that size pays the resize cost. I'd also mention request collapsing for the case where a redesign suddenly makes many images need a new size at once — without it, that moment spikes the resize workers.

**Testing:** whether you can justify a hybrid strategy with the actual trade-off, not just name both options.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Precompute vs on-the-fly derivatives
